title: Friends and social life
intro: How Spanish handles invitations, arrangements and company. Note quedar for making plans (unit 1) and invitar, which in Latin America usually means to pay as well as to invite.

entries.note: See unit 3. el conocido is an acquaintance; el compañero a colleague or classmate.

ex.es: Salí con unos amigos del trabajo.
ex.en: I went out with some friends from work.

entries.en: to invite; to treat, to pay for
entries.note: Yo invito means my treat. Saying te invito un café offers to buy it.

ex.en: They invited us to their wedding.
It's my treat today.
Thank you for the invitation.

entries.note: ¿Tienes planes? asks about your plans. hacer planes is to make plans.

ex.en: What are your plans for Saturday?

entries.note: ¿Te acompaño? offers to come with you.

ex.en: I'll walk you to the station.

entries.en: to meet someone, to get to know someone
entries.note: See unit 1. The past conocí means I met, for the first time.

ex.en: I met her at a party.

entries.note: te presento a Ana is how you introduce someone.

ex.en: Let me introduce you to my sister.

ex.es: Presentó su trabajo en la reunión.
ex.en: She presented her work at the meeting.

entries.en: to greet, to say hello; to say goodbye
entries.note: el saludo is a greeting; la despedida a farewell or leaving party.

ex.en: He walked past without saying hello.
She said goodbye to everyone.

entries.note: los novios are the couple at a wedding. See unit 10 for la pareja.

ex.en: He came with his girlfriend.
The bride and groom arrived late.

entries.en: to go out with, to date
entries.note: salir alone is simply to go out — see unit 22.

ex.en: They've been going out since March.

entries.en: to argue, to discuss; to fight, to quarrel
entries.note: discutir leans towards arguing, not calm discussion. For that use hablar de or tratar.

ex.en: We argued over something silly.

ex.es: Los niños pelean todo el día.
ex.en: The children fight all day.

entries.note: perdón is the noun and the apology — see unit 5.

ex.en: She never forgave him.
He promised me he'd come.

entries.en: to let know, to warn, to notify
entries.note: avísame means let me know. Extremely common and has no neat English single word.

ex.en: Let me know when you arrive.

entries.note: See unit 7. Social life in the Spanish-speaking world is organised around both.

ex.en: See you at dinner.
It was a very long meal.

entries.en: to toast, to drink a toast
entries.note: brindar por is to drink to something. See salud in unit 5.

ex.en: Let's drink to the bride and groom.

entries.note: See unit 3. In small towns the vecinos are effectively an institution.

ex.en: My neighbours are very kind.

entries.note: sólo with an accent used to mean only; the accent is now optional and usually dropped.

ex.en: We studied together at university.
He prefers to work alone.

entries.note: hacer un favor is to do a favour; por favor is please — see unit 5.

ex.en: Would you do me a favour?

entries.note: tener confianza con alguien is to be close enough to speak freely.

ex.en: He lost his trust in them.
We're very close.
